name: Erik Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run three CNC lathes at a small engineering firm on the industrial estate, about forty of us, making brass and steel hydraulic fittings. CNC means the lathe is controlled by a computer program, so my job is loading bar stock, swapping tools when they wear, measuring parts with a micrometer and keeping the coolant topped up. I'm not the programmer, but I can tweak an offset when a size drifts. Most days I'm running two machines while the third one's being set.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment the first good part comes off after a changeover, when the gauge says it's spot on. What wears me out is the pay, which is below what the bigger firms in the city pay, and the long bus ride if I miss my lift with Tomas. I live with my partner Jun, who's doing a nursing degree, so I'm the main earner for now and we've got maybe three weeks of money saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the hype was overblown, but the tools are still handy. At work I'd keep showing people how I use the chatbot to check a drawing. Online I'd probably post that the real story is still wages and housing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a bit disappointing, because I was hoping AI would push our boss to pay for better training. Without a shake-up, I'm stuck on lower pay in a small firm with nowhere else nearby. Jun's degree is two more years, and we're just scraping by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to learn programming for the lathes in the evenings, because that's the better-paid job. I'd ask the boss if I can shadow Viktor, our programmer, one afternoon a week. I'd pick up weekend repair jobs on bikes for a bit of extra cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about AI, not calm about money. The future looks the same, and the same isn't great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools every day. What do you actually use them for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask it to explain the G-code, which is the list of instructions the lathe runs, and to check my tolerance maths before I trust it. I've learned more about lathe programming from a chatbot on the night bus than in two years at the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're the main earner while Jun studies. What happens if your hours drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're in real trouble, because Jun's student loan doesn't cover rent. I'd do more bike repairs and we'd cut food right down. It's happened before, when the firm lost a big order for a month.

say: I'd say the **hype** was overblown, but the tools are still handy.
I'd post that the real story is still **wages and housing**.
think: I think it's **disappointing**, because a shake-up might have forced better training.
I think I'm **stuck** on lower pay with Jun's degree still two years off.
do: Learn **lathe programming** with AI in the evenings.
Ask to shadow **Viktor**, the programmer, one afternoon a week.
Take weekend **bike repair** jobs for extra cash.
feel: **Calm about AI**, but not calm about money.
S0.quote: I've learned more about lathe programming from a chatbot on the night bus than in two years at the firm.
fieldNote: Erik is the **main earner** while Jun studies, which keeps him anxious even with no AI change.
He uses AI daily as a **self-teaching tool** for programming.
He sees the real fight as **wages and housing**, not technology.

steps.text: Learn CNC lathe programming with AI tools in the evenings
Ask to shadow Viktor the programmer one afternoon a week
Fix bikes on weekends for extra cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, if workers get trained properly and not just binned. At work I'd be the one setting up the AI tool on the shop computer for everyone. Online I'd say the companies saving money should pay for the training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm in a decent spot, because I already use the tools and I'm learning to program. The quoting and ordering in the office will shrink, but someone still has to load the lathes for a while. My worry is the boss buying a robot loader before I've made the jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard to get on the programming side, maybe offer to write the setup sheets with AI for free at first. I'd look at an evening course in robotics at the college, which is about 300 for a term. I'd try to get the shop's few workers to join the union, because nobody's in one right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and nervous in about equal parts. Like the start of a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In this picture, thinking work like planning and ordering goes first. What does that do to your small firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boss would use AI to quote jobs and order steel, and he'd stop hiring an office assistant. Then he'd look at the floor and think about a robot to load bar stock at night. A robot that loads lathes overnight would pay for itself in eighteen months, and my boss can do that maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think people like you will get a fair shot at the new jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if someone makes sure of it. Firms like ours don't train anyone unless they have to. That's why I'd want the union in, and the government paying for courses.

I'd say companies saving money should **pay for training**.
think: I think I'm in a **decent spot** because I already use the tools.
I think the risk is a **robot loader** before I've made the jump.

fieldNote: Erik sees opportunity, but his **thin savings** and a possible robot loader keep him anxious.
He would organise a **union** in a shop that has none.
He frames it as a race to make **the jump** before the boss buys robots.

steps.text: Write lathe setup sheets with AI to move toward programming

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency help for workers, like what happened during the pandemic, and a tax on the companies that profit. At work I'd tell the lads to learn everything they can about the robots. Online I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, that one's scary, because the programming I'm learning is the thinking part that goes first, in 2028. So my plan to be the programmer falls apart. What's left is the hands-on side, fixing and fitting robots, until they can do that too around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch straight to robot maintenance, the hands-on side, because that lasts three years longer. I'd ask the robot supplier if they need installers, because they'll be rushed off their feet. I'd join whatever union or campaign is pushing for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground tilted. My whole plan pointed the wrong way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028, robots by about 2031. The programming side is thinking work. Does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The programming used to be the safe job, and the hands were the risky one. In AGI by 2028, the lathe programming I'm learning goes first, and my hands are the last thing worth paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With Jun still studying, what would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going out, then the bus pass, I'd cycle. We'd talk about Jun pausing the degree, but I'd fight that, because nurses will still be needed. I'd rather do nights at the supplier than make Jun stop.

say: I'd say workers need **emergency help** and the companies that profit should pay.
I'd tell colleagues to learn everything about the **robots**.
think: I think the **programming** I'm learning is the thinking part that goes first.
I think the **hands-on side** buys me about three more years.
do: Switch straight to **robot maintenance**, the hands-on side.
Ask the **robot supplier** if they need installers.
Join a campaign for a **basic income**.
feel: Like the **ground tilted** and my plan pointed the wrong way.
S2.quote: In AGI by 2028, the lathe programming I'm learning goes first, and my hands are the last thing worth paying for.
fieldNote: Erik spots that the **thinking-first** order flips his career plan, which surprised me.
He'd protect **Jun's nursing degree** above his own comfort.
He'd move fast but still expects to lose most of his income by **2031**.

steps.text: Switch from lathe programming to robot maintenance training
Ask the robot supplier for installer work
Join a campaign for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do this right, with proper retraining and a fair share for workers. At work I'd keep pushing people to get skilled up. Online I'd talk about what a fair deal looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is long enough to get qualified as a robot technician and get a few years of better pay before the end. Jun would be a qualified nurse by then, so we'd have two incomes. That changes a lot for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics course part-time for two years and look for a technician job at a bigger plant. I'd save hard once Jun's working, aiming for three months. I'd keep using AI every day to learn faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, honestly. Worried about the end, but hopeful about the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still learn to program, knowing it goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, because knowing the code helps you fix the robot. I'd learn just enough to understand it, but put my time into the hands-on side, and switch again when that changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes at home over those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to become a robot technician and for Jun (his partner) to start nursing, so we'd finally have two wages. That would be the first time we've had any slack at all.

say: I'd say there's time to do this **right**, with proper retraining.
I'd talk online about what a **fair deal** for workers looks like.
think: I think five years gets me **qualified** as a robot technician.
I think **Jun's wage** as a nurse would change everything for us.
do: Do the **robotics course** part-time over two years.
Look for a **technician job** at a bigger plant.
Save hard for **three months** of costs once Jun is working.
feel: **Hopeful** about the middle years, worried about the end.
S3.quote: Five years is enough for me to become a robot technician and for Jun (his partner) to start nursing, so we'd finally have two wages.
fieldNote: The five-year window lines up with **Jun qualifying**, which lifts Erik's mood.
He'd keep only **enough coding** to understand robots and focus on hands-on repair.
He expects to keep earning through the change, so he's **uneasy**, not anxious.

steps.text: Do the robotics course part-time over two years
Apply for robot technician jobs at bigger plants
Save three months of costs once Jun is nursing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so the government should set up proper paid retraining for everyone. At work I'd say let's all get trained before it's urgent. Online I'd share the courses that are actually worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of that one. I'd have time to get qualified, move up and save, and Jun would be a nurse for years. I'd still worry about the end, but not for a long while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics qualification steadily over three years and maybe start a small business repairing machines for small firms. I'd keep learning AI tools. I'd get a union going at whatever plant I end up in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. Like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any downside to having that much time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Too much time can make you lazy, and people say there's no rush. With ten years of warning, the danger is my mates on the shop floor thinking there's no rush until the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about Tomas and the older lads, honestly, more than me. They wouldn't move until they had to.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, and paid retraining should be set up now.
I'd share the **courses** that are actually worth doing.
think: I think I'd **do well**, with time to qualify and save.
I think the end still worries me, but **not for years**.
do: Get the **robotics qualification** steadily over three years.
Start a small **repair business** for local firms' machines.
Set up a **union** at whatever plant I end up in.
S4.quote: With ten years of warning, the danger is my mates on the shop floor thinking there's no rush until the robots arrive.
fieldNote: With a decade, Erik is **calm**, because he expects to move up before robots arrive.
His concern shifts to **older colleagues** who won't move until forced.
He combines **adaptability** with a strong sense of collective fairness.

steps.text: Complete the robotics qualification over three years

Set up a union at his next plant

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the thing I'm learning goes first and I've got no savings to change course twice. What would help is free, paid retraining that you can get fast, and a basic income for the gap. Give me six months on half pay to learn robot maintenance, and I'd be the most useful person on the industrial estate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about small firms. Big plants have training budgets, but places like ours have nothing, and that's where most of us work.

headlineQuote: Give me six months on half pay to learn robot maintenance, and I'd be the most useful person on the industrial estate.
portrait: Erik, 27, runs **three CNC lathes** at a 40-person firm and is the main earner while his partner Jun studies nursing.
He uses **AI every day** to teach himself lathe programming and wants better-paid, skilled work.
He is **progressive**, keen on unions, and wants companies and government to fund retraining.
He is **alarmed** in AGI by 2028 because his programming plan goes first, but **calm** with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his chosen skill goes first and he can't afford to switch twice.
whatWouldHelp: Fast, **paid retraining** and a **basic income** to cover the gap.
